strengths: The paper offers a useful perspective on black-box model provenance: restricting watermarking to a selectable domain can preserve general utility while allowing targeted fingerprint queries.

Experiments span two model families, three natural domains, several capability benchmarks, and multiple finetuning datasets. Results, particularly for French fingerprints, provide encouraging evidence of detectability and persistence.
The appendices add valuable experiments on watermark strength, context length, greedy decoding, domain leakage, and multiple keys, exposing tradeoffs beyond the main results.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not convincingly establish superiority over prior fingerprinting methods. Appendix A.3 replaces scalable fingerprinting's model merging with weight decay, changing the evaluated method. Baselines are assessed through per-query exact-match rates or a majority criterion, whereas the proposed method aggregates evidence across many queries. Repeated queries can also improve backdoor detection, contrary to the paper's categorical claim. Comparisons need faithful implementations and matched query budgets and false-positive rates; persistence results for KGW-D are also missing.

Persistence claims exceed the evidence. In Table 3, both Math fingerprints remain at 0.50 accuracy after in-domain finetuning and 1,000 queries; Qwen Health reaches only 0.60. Qwen Math also remains at 0.50 after Alpaca finetuning, an out-of-domain setting. These results contradict claims of near-perfect recovery across settings. Arbitrarily increasing detection power requires a surviving positive signal and appropriate aggregation assumptions; increasing query count alone does not guarantee recovery.

The claimed formal false-positive guarantees are insufficiently established. Section 3 moves from an asymptotic normal approximation to a guarantee at alpha = 1e-5 without a finite-sample justification for the implemented detector. Average null p-values near 0.5 do not establish calibration in this extreme tail. The assumptions and handling of repeated contexts across aggregated responses require clearer specification and validation.

Quality preservation is conditional and sometimes incomplete. For Llama, French watermarking lowers the in-domain judge score from 6.00 to 3.33, while Math watermarking lowers it from 8.33 to 4.67. Even outside the target domain, Qwen Math increases general-Q&A perplexity from 4.73 to 5.68. These tradeoffs deserve more qualified claims than 'harmless' or broadly quality-preserving fingerprints.

Stealthiness is supported primarily by selected examples, without a quantitative distinguishability or query-filtering evaluation. Three benign system prompts and greedy decoding provide useful deployment checks, but do not establish robustness against an adversary with access to released weights. Quantization, explicitly mentioned in the threat model, and adaptive removal or evasion are not evaluated.

The technical contribution is principally domain-conditioned application of existing KGW distillation. Ablations do not isolate the contribution of domain restriction from regularization or compare alternative regularizers. Moreover, if Equation (4) is summed over vocabulary entries to obtain a scalar, its positive-deviation expression is exactly standard total variation distance, rather than a distinct variant.

Reproducibility and reporting need correction: the setup and examples identify Qwen-7B while tables identify Qwen-3B; Appendix B contradicts the main watermark context-length setting; and the regularization coefficient lambda is unspecified. Uncertainty across independent training runs and watermark keys is also not established.

The method is straightforward and technically plausible, combining KGW watermark distillation with reference-model regularization without requiring inference-time modifications.
Experiments across two model families and three domains show promising detection, preservation of many out-of-domain capabilities, and persistence under several fine-tuning conditions.
The appendices provide useful additional investigations, including fingerprinting baselines, greedy decoding, watermark hyperparameters, multiple keys, and domain leakage.
weaknesses: The baseline comparisons do not convincingly establish superiority. Appendices A.2–A.3 emphasize per-response exact-match rates, whereas the proposed method aggregates evidence across queries. Repeated querying can also improve backdoor detection. Moreover, the scalable-fingerprint implementation replaces the original model merging with weight decay and uses an inadequately justified majority-match decision rule. Comparisons need matched query budgets and false-positive rates.

The central persistence advantage over conventional watermark distillation is not directly demonstrated: KGW-D is evaluated for quality but is absent from the corresponding fine-tuning persistence comparison. Ablations separating domain restriction, regularization, and query aggregation are needed to identify the source of improvement.

Persistence claims exceed the reported results. In Table 3, both Math fingerprints retain only 0.50 accuracy after in-domain fine-tuning even with 1,000 queries; Qwen Math also obtains 0.50 after Alpaca fine-tuning, and Qwen Health reaches only 0.60 after health fine-tuning. These failures contradict broad claims of near-perfect recovery and persistence across all evaluated settings. Increasing query count cannot guarantee recovery without a surviving positive signal.

The claimed formal false-positive guarantee is stronger than the statistical analysis supports. Equation (1) uses an asymptotic normal approximation, which does not establish finite-sample control at 1e-5. Average null p-values near 0.5 do not validate the relevant tail. The paper needs a justified calibration procedure, explicit handling of repeated contexts across responses, and clearer evidence across independent keys and null models.

Quality preservation is substantially conditional on domain. Table 1 shows Llama French perplexity increasing from 4.38 to 11.1 and its judge score falling from 6.00 to 3.33. There are also out-of-domain losses, such as Qwen Math's general-Q&A perplexity increasing from 4.73 to 5.68. These tradeoffs need more balanced treatment, and qualitative examples do not establish the claimed inherent stealthiness.

Technical novelty beyond selective application of established watermark distillation is modest. When summed over vocabulary, the positive-deviation regularizer in Equation (4) is ordinary total variation, rather than a distinct asymmetric variant. Comparisons against KL regularization and removal of the regularizer would strengthen the methodological contribution.

The deployment and adversarial claims have limited support. Three benign system prompts, greedy decoding, and one fine-tuning recipe do not establish broad robustness; quantization is mentioned in the threat model but not evaluated. Calling in-domain fine-tuning an adversarial worst case is unjustified. Watermark detection also establishes signal association, rather than uniquely proving that particular model weights are being served; transfer through watermarked training data is not addressed.

Reporting inconsistencies and missing details impede reproducibility. Section 5 identifies Qwen2.5-7B, while the principal tables and figures identify Qwen2.5-3B. Appendix B contradicts the main setup and its own table about watermark hyperparameters. The regularization coefficient, domain-filtering procedure, and variability across training seeds and watermark keys are insufficiently specified.

Under Appendix A.2's any-hit detection rule, a 5% success probability gives approximately 99.4% detection within 100 independent queries. Thus, existing fingerprints can also benefit from additional queries. Appendix A.3 additionally replaces the published model-merging procedure with weight decay without validating equivalence. The claimed formal false-positive guarantee is not established. Equation (1) uses an asymptotic normal approximation at a nominal threshold of 1e-5. Even under an ideal independent Binomial(200, 0.25) null, its rejection threshold has an exact tail probability of approximately 1.73e-5. Cross-query deduplication and dependence also need precise treatment. Average null p-values near 0.5 do not validate extreme-tail calibration; an exact or conservative test, or a justified calibration analysis, is needed.

Harmlessness and stealthiness require stronger qualification. Three benign system prompts, limited decoding checks, and one fine-tuning schedule do not establish robustness across realistic modifications. Quantization appears explicitly in the threat model but is not evaluated. Ordinary same-domain fine-tuning is also not demonstrated to constitute an adversarial worst case.

The incremental contribution over existing KGW distillation is insufficiently isolated. Additionally, Equation (4), if summed over the vocabulary, is exactly total variation distance rather than a distinct asymmetric variant.

Appendix B identifies the reference context length as h=2, whereas the main setup and highlighted Table 9 row use h=1. Average benchmark accuracy and out-of-domain generation quality are largely preserved. The manuscript provides substantial implementation detail and states that code accompanies the submission.
weaknesses: The minimal-utility-impact claim is overstated. Table 4 reports French generation-quality scores falling from 5.10 to 3.18, 6.47 to 5.12, and 6.90 to 4.82. These are substantial reductions in the domain used for fingerprinting. Although acknowledged in the appendix, they undermine the main presentation. Lower watermark strengths are explored, but their robustness under the full attack suite is not established.

The stealth evaluation is insufficient for a central claim. A generic GPT5-MINI classifier instructed to avoid false positives provides limited evidence against informed adversaries. The paper does not evaluate domain discovery or the cited targeted watermark-detection techniques. Keeping a common language such as French secret is an assumption requiring stronger empirical justification.

The incremental benefit over ordinary watermark distillation is not cleanly isolated. Appendix B.3 evaluates full watermarking only on one model under a limited finetuning comparison; its average signal also exceeds the detection threshold at the main query budget. The comparison changes French training exposure and does not match initial watermark strength or utility, confounding the claimed robustness advantage of semantic conditioning.

Baseline comparisons need additional validation. Appendix A.2 adapts completion-oriented methods to chat models, and SF detection requires exact matches to long generated replies. This can amplify sensitivity to system prompts and paraphrasing. Sensitivity analyses and validation of the adapted implementations would strengthen the conclusion that the observed failures characterize the underlying methods.

Statistical reliability is overstated. FSR uses only five detection runs per setting, without reported variation across independently trained fingerprints or keys. Zero observed false positives does not empirically validate an FPR of 0.001. Appendix D provides an asymptotic justification, but its context-diversity condition and finite-sample calibration are not checked.

Several technical reporting issues require correction: Equations (3) and (8) use inconsistent variance normalizations; Table 4 reports perplexities below one, which is impossible for conventional perplexity; and the experimental details omit the regularization weight lambda. These appear correctable but reduce confidence in reproducibility.

strengths: The central idea is useful and well motivated: semantically conditioned watermarks allow fingerprint evidence to accumulate across natural responses instead of depending on exact query–response matches.

The evaluation covers three models, eight utility benchmarks, and numerous deployment modifications, including quantization, pruning, finetuning, and adversarial paraphrasing. The reported detection results are consistently strong.

The appendices provide valuable ablations of query count, watermark strength, semantic domain, regularization, and unconditional watermarking, alongside exploratory demonstrations of token-controlled watermarks.
weaknesses: The minimal-utility-impact claim substantially understates the paper's own evidence. Table 4 reports French response-quality declines from 5.10 to 3.18, 6.47 to 5.12, and 6.90 to 4.82 across the three models. Stable aggregate benchmark accuracy does not resolve these substantial losses. Lower watermark strengths are explored, but their robustness–quality tradeoff is not evaluated across the main deployment suite.

The statistical evidence does not establish the advertised reliability. Five detection trials per setting cannot validate a false-positive rate of 0.001 or near-perfect success across independently trained fingerprints and keys. Theorem D.1 provides an asymptotic result under context-diversity assumptions that are not checked experimentally. Furthermore, Equation (3) and Equations (8)–(10) use inconsistent powers of the correction factor beta.

The stealth evaluation is too weak for the central claim. A single generically prompted LLM judge, with English Alpaca negatives and French fingerprint queries, does not establish resistance to domain-matched classifiers, aggregate query monitoring, or adaptive domain discovery. The acknowledged dependence on domain secrecy requires stronger evaluation. Round-trip input translation also preserves the French trigger before inference, leaving translation into an unmarked domain untested.

Baseline adaptations complicate interpretation. Appendix A.2 evaluates SF using exact matches to entire generated responses after modifying its construction for instruction-tuned models. Added acknowledgments or other formatting changes can therefore cause failure without demonstrating that the underlying fingerprint information disappeared. Comparisons should verify that the adapted detection procedures preserve the intended capabilities of the original methods.

The closest watermark-based comparator receives incomplete evaluation. Appendix B.3 is useful, but Figure 4 shows that unconditional watermarking also remains detectable within the 1,000-query budget after the tested finetuning. Comparisons across the full deployment suite, with matched utility and embedding budgets, are needed to isolate the benefits of semantic conditioning.

Several reporting issues weaken reproducibility: the regularization coefficient lambda is unspecified, and Table 4 reports perplexities below one, which are impossible under the standard definition. Together with the detector inconsistency, these require clarification before the quantitative claims can be assessed confidently.
